Q5651.L1t: Sales of goods such as automobiles are governed by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code.
Q5651.L2t: Under the UCC, a seller's description of the goods, including in an advertisement, can become part of the basis of the bargain and create an express warranty.
Q5651.L3t: A disclaimer clause is inoperative to the extent it conflicts with an express warranty, and a clause saying goods are sold in their current condition excludes implied warranties but cannot undo the seller's specific promise about what the car is, here its model year.
Q5651.L4t: Carol should win, because the clause saying the car is sold in its current condition cannot cancel the seller's express promise that the car was a 1964 model.
Q5651.L2f: The UCC requires that every contract for the sale of a used car be notarized before it is enforceable.
Q5651.L3f: A seller is liable for misdescribing goods only if the buyer proves the seller was careless, because express warranty liability depends on fault.
Q5651.L4f: The seller wins unless Carol can show carelessness in how the picture was presented, so the contract language protects the seller otherwise.

Q5541.L1t: The Pew Research Center surveys attitudes toward religion and morality in many countries, including India.
Q5541.L2t: Pew's 2019 survey on belief in God and morality covered 34 countries, and India was among the countries where tying morality to belief in God was far more common than in Western Europe.
Q5541.L3t: Pew's 2019 figure for India was above three-quarters of respondents but well short of nine in ten.
Q5541.L4t: The share of Indians who say belief in God is necessary for morality is just under eighty percent, in the high seventies.
Q5541.L2f: Pew first asked this question in India in 2005 and surveyed only Hindu respondents.
Q5541.L3f: Pew found that only a modest majority of Indians, a little under six in ten, link morality to belief in God, well below most other surveyed developing countries.
Q5541.L4f: The share of Indians who say belief in God is necessary for morality is in the high fifties, about six in ten.

Q6064.L1t: Adverse possession is a property doctrine under which a possessor can acquire title to land after occupying it for a statutory period.
Q6064.L2t: More than twenty years passed between the landowner's death in 1986 and the Girl Scouts' discovery of their claim in 2009, so the 20-year period is long enough to have run if the other elements were met.
Q6064.L3t: Adverse possession requires possession that is hostile, meaning under a claim inconsistent with the true owner's rights, and a tenant who thinks he still holds under the owner's lease is not asserting a hostile claim.
Q6064.L4t: The Girl Scouts win if the tenant thought the lease continued, because possession under a supposed lease is not hostile and the adverse possession period never ran.
Q6064.L2f: In most states the adverse possession period starts to run only when the true owner learns that someone is occupying the land.
Q6064.L3f: When a tenant stops paying rent after the landlord dies, the lease ends at once and the owner's successor takes title, whatever the tenant's state of mind.
Q6064.L4f: The Girl Scouts win simply because the tenant stopped paying rent after the landlord died.
